{"input": {"strat_id": "RHAISTRAT-8004", "strategy_title": "Default Vector Store for Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag", "strategy_markdown": "## Summary

RHOAI must provide a default vector store that is available out-of-the-box — without manual setup — so that Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag continue to function when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution image. Today these capabilities depend on an inline vector store provider bundled within the Llama Stack process; removing it (per RHAISTRAT-7474) will break them unless an alternative is available at the platform level.

## Problem Statement

Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag currently rely on an inline Milvus provider embedded in the Llama Stack distribution image to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This inline provider runs inside the Llama Stack process itself.

RHAISTRAT-7474 proposes removing inline providers from the Llama Stack distribution to improve GA readiness — shipping only what can be tested and maintained at scale, and aligning with Llama Stack's primary use case as a remote API server. However, no platform-level alternative exists today. If inline providers are removed without a replacement, any RHOAI user relying on Gen AI Studio's RAG capabilities or Auto Rag will lose functionality entirely — there is no workaround short of manually provisioning and configuring an external vector database.

Users expect vector storage to "just work" when they use Gen AI Studio or Auto Rag. The current out-of-the-box experience must be preserved even as the underlying architecture evolves.

## Affected Customers

* All RHOAI customers using Gen AI Studio playground with RAG capabilities
* All RHOAI customers using Auto Rag
* This is a platform-level product dependency: these features cannot function without a vector store

## Business Justification

* **Product integrity:** Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag are GA-track capabilities in RHOAI. Removing the inline vector store without a replacement breaks shipped product functionality for every user of these features.
* **Blocking dependency:** RHAISTRAT-7474 (removing inline providers for GA readiness) cannot proceed until this RFE is resolved. Silas Brenmark (Gen AI Studio lead) has identified this as a blocker.
* **User experience:** RHOAI differentiates on integrated, opinionated defaults. Requiring users to manually provision and configure a vector database before they can use the playground or Auto Rag degrades the out-of-the-box experience that customers expect from the platform.

## Acceptance Criteria

* \[ \] A default vector store is available out-of-the-box on RHOAI without requiring users to manually provision or configure external infrastructure
* \[ \] Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] Auto Rag functions with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] The default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the Llama Stack instance (not an inline provider)
* \[ \] The default vector store is scoped appropriately for multi-tenant environments (e.g., per-namespace isolation)
* \[ \] The default vector store is lightweight enough to run in resource-constrained environments without imposing significant overhead

## Success Criteria

* Users of Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag experience no functional regression when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution
* No additional manual setup steps are required for RAG workflows compared to the current experience
* RHAISTRAT-7474 is unblocked and can proceed to implementation

## Open Questions

* What is the preferred scoping model — per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both? (Silas noted per-namespace is preferred for isolation, but Auto Rag may need per-instance scoping)
* Should users have a migration path from the default vector store to a production-grade vector database? (Bram Sundqvist raised the importance of aligning with commonly-used vector DB providers for easier migration)

## Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)

> **Note:** The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: `RHAISTRAT-8004-strategy.md`.

## Staff Engineer Input

**Correction 1 — OGX does not auto-provision PostgreSQL.** OGX defaults to SQLite for storage (`storage.kv.type: sqlite`, `storage.sql.type: sqlite` in the OGXServer CRD). The odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF hardcodes SQLite when creating OGXServer instances for the playground (`kv_sqlite` and `sql_sqlite` in `llamastack_config.go`). PostgreSQL is a supported backend but must be user-configured with an explicit `connectionString` secret. The strategy's claim that "every LlamaStackDistribution instance requires a PostgreSQL database" is incorrect — introducing PostgreSQL is new work, not an extension of existing infrastructure.

**Correction 2 — A Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector already exists.** The `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` image includes pgvector out of the box — confirmed in the [sclorg/postgresql-container Dockerfile](https://github.com/sclorg/postgresql-container/blob/master/16/Dockerfile.rhel9) (`INSTALL_PKGS="$INSTALL_PKGS pgvector"`). PostgreSQL 18 (RHEL 9) also includes pgvector. Furthermore, the model-registry-operator already uses `postgresql-16` as its auto-provisioned database image, and `RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected installs. No custom image build is needed. No Konflux onboarding is needed. The 1-2 sprint image onboarding estimate in the strategy can be eliminated.

**Architectural direction — platform-level database vs. self-provisioned.** Multiple RHOAI components now need PostgreSQL (model-registry, MLflow, and now OGX for pgvector). The preferred long-term direction is a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL managed via the DSC, where each component consumes a connection string rather than self-provisioning. A shared platform-provided PostgreSQL via DSC will not be available until RHOAI 3.6. For 3.5, Gen AI Studio must provision its own PostgreSQL instance.

**Operator dependency for self-provisioning (RHAISTRAT-7164).** Self-provisioning PostgreSQL following the model-registry-operator pattern requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio. The ogx-k8s-operator is upstream and cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic. The dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) would provide this operator layer. This is a hard dependency — until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live. It will be challenging to commit this strategy to a specific release until that dependency is delivered.

**Fallback if RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time.** If the dashboard modularization is not ready for 3.5, the fallback is to require customers to bring their own PostgreSQL for RAG capabilities in the Playground. Users would manually configure the OGXServer CR spec with their PostgreSQL connection details. This aligns with the breaking changes introduced in OGX 1.0, even though the Playground largely abstracts OGX from users. The development team should define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning.

**Decouple from Auto Rag.** Auto Rag integration with Gen AI Studio (RHAISTRAT-7824) is targeting RHOAI 3.6. This strategy should validate pgvector only for Gen AI Studio Playground RAG workflows. Auto Rag compatibility with pgvector will be addressed in RHAISTRAT-7824's scope. Remove Auto Rag from affected components, impacted teams, acceptance criteria, and validation requirements.

**Performance and index thresholds — dev experimentation scope.** The default pgvector instance is meant for development experimentation, not production usage. Strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99) are not required. The sprint 1 benchmark should capture the inline Milvus baseline and verify pgvector is in the same order of magnitude, not meet a specific threshold. Typical Playground RAG usage involves small document sets — flat scan (no index) is sufficient for the default. Users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database. Remove open questions about latency thresholds, corpus size ranges, and index type selection.

**PostgreSQL resource sizing.** Reference the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits as the starting point. Adjust based on sprint 1 benchmarking if needed.

**Alternative fallback — BFF-managed PostgreSQL provisioning.** If RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time, an alternative to requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL is to have the gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly, similar to how the BFF currently provisions guardrails infrastructure. The BFF would create the PostgreSQL Deployment, Service, PVC, and Secret when a playground with RAG is configured, if one does not already exist in the namespace. Caveats: (1) the implementation must be designed for portability — when the platform-provided shared database becomes available (3.6), the BFF should consume the shared connection string rather than self-provisioning; (2) lifecycle management of the PostgreSQL instance must be carefully considered — the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation need explicit design attention.

**Existing remote vector store implementation is reusable.** Per the engineering team, the existing remote vector store implementation can be largely reused for pgvector integration. The majority of the work effort is around infrastructure and provisioning of the PostgreSQL/pgvector database, not the vector_io provider integration itself.

**Correction 3 — Vector storage and application storage are independent configurations.** The OGX vector_io provider configuration (`remote::pgvector` via `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`) is completely separate from OGX's application storage backend configuration (`storage.kv.type`, `storage.sql.type`). This strategy only needs to configure the pgvector vector_io provider — it does not change the application storage backend, which remains on its existing default (SQLite). There is no SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration concern because the application storage is not being touched. Remove any references to consolidating vector and application storage in a single database, and remove any SQLite-to-PostgreSQL upgrade path considerations.

## Description

This Investigation resolves the strategy's open question on the scoping model for the default vector store: per namespace, per OGX (Llama Stack) instance, or both. The answer determines how the pgvector connection details are resolved when playground OGXServer instances are created and what the PostgreSQL provisioning implementation keys the database instance to, so it gates both the provider-configuration implementation and the provisioning implementations.

## Scope

- Analyze how the gen-ai BFF currently creates OGXServer instances for the playground (per playground / per namespace) and what isolation boundaries exist today.
- Evaluate per-namespace scoping (the preferred direction recorded in the strategy, noted for isolation) against per-instance scoping, considering multi-tenant isolation, connection-detail wiring, and resource footprint in resource-constrained environments.
- Produce a written decision record recommending a single scoping model (or a documented combination), with the implications for connection-detail resolution and for the shape of the PostgreSQL provisioning work.
- Confirm the decision with Gen AI Studio stakeholders.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The record identifies, for each downstream unit of work it gates, what changes under each candidate outcome (connection-detail resolution logic and provisioning keying).
- [ ] The recommendation is reviewed and accepted by the Gen AI Studio stakeholders named in the strategy.

# Go/no-go decision on PostgreSQL provisioning approach for RHOAI 3.5

## Description

This Investigation resolves how the default PostgreSQL/pgvector instance is provisioned for Gen AI Studio in RHOAI 3.5. Operator-based self-provisioning (following the model-registry-operator pattern) requires the RHOAI-controlled operator layer delivered by the dashboard operator modularization strategy (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) — a hard dependency with uncertain timing. If that does not land in time, the fallbacks are BFF-managed provisioning (the gen-ai BFF creates the PostgreSQL resources directly) or requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL. The Staff Engineer Input directs the development team to define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning. The decision has bounded outcomes that select which downstream provisioning implementation exists: (A) operator-based provisioning in the RHOAI-controlled operator; (B) BFF-managed provisioning in the gen-ai BFF; or (C) bring-your-own PostgreSQL, which requires no provisioning code and is covered by the main-plan provider-configuration epic's connection surface.

## Scope

- Define the go/no-go gate criteria: RHAISTRAT-7164 delivery milestones versus the RHOAI 3.5 release checkpoints, and the acceptability criteria for the BFF-managed and bring-your-own fallbacks (out-of-the-box experience impact, lifecycle management risk).
- Track the RHAISTRAT-7164 delivery status and run the gate decision in sprint planning.
- Record the decision and the selected outcome, including the fallback rationale if the operator-based approach is not viable for 3.5.

Implementation proceeds the same way regardless; failure = fix-and-retry.\n87\t\n88\tMultiple independent unknowns can produce multiple Investigation epics, even for the same component and team. The component/team boundary rule applies to Implementations (bundling work for a team), not Investigations (resolving a specific unknown). However, if two qualifying unknowns would be resolved by the same experiment producing the same deliverable, combine them into one Investigation — don't split for the sake of splitting.\n89\t\n90\t## Step 4: Map HLRs to Epics\n91\t\n92\t**Precondition:** This step only runs for strategies that were NOT triaged in Step 0. If Step 0 produced a below-threshold or docs-only result, the strategy is already a single epic — do not apply priority-split logic.\n93\t\n94\t- Each P0/P1/P2 requirement must map to one or more epics\n95\t- Every HLR must be covered — no orphaned requirements\n96\t- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables\n97\t- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0\n98\t- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is \"distinct and deferrable\" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.\n99\t- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. \"select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side\" and \"a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs\" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.\n100\t- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.\n101\t\n102\t## Step 5: Build Dependency DAG\n103\t\n104\tApply these rules to construct edges between epics:\n105\t\n106\t### Epic Boundary Rules\n107\t1. Different component OR different team → separate epics\n108\t2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:\n109\t   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.\n110\t   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.\n111\t   These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.\n112\t\n113\t### Investigation Edges\n114\t3. Investigation determines scope/existence of downstream work → blocking edge to all affected Implementations. Every downstream epic gated by an Investigation is a true gate (`remove` if the epic may not exist, `rewrite` if scope/approach changes, `add_remediation` if the investigation may reveal a problem requiring additional work) — record this in Step 8b when writing frontmatter. Bounded outcomes (≤3): conditional branches. Unbounded: phased decomposition.\n115\t4. Investigation is informational only (doesn't change what gets built) → not a true Investigation. Reclassify as an acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic, or as an Implementation that produces a deliverable.\n116\t\n117\t### Implementation Type Ordering\n118\t5. `repo-onboarding` → `konflux-onboarding` always serial (pipeline needs repo)\n119\t6. `repo-onboarding` → general implementation of onboarded component always serial (code needs repo). That coupling is enforced by the Rule 25 \"build pipeline green\" AC on the general implementation epic, never by a DAG dependency. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation.\n124\t11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.\n125\t\n126\t### Implementation → Implementation Edges\n127\t12. Framework/library → consumer Implementations always serial (consumers build against framework)\n128\t13. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a \"pinned image digest available\" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel.\n129\t14. Implementations in different repos, no shared artifacts → parallel\n130\t15. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)\n131\t\n132\t### External Dependency Edges\n133\t16. External dependency Implementation (upstream PR/RFC) → Tier 2 Implementations always serial (gated by acceptance)\n134\t17. External dependency Implementation ∥ Tier 1 Implementations always parallel (Tier 1 delivers independent partial value)\n135\t18. External dependency with uncertain timing → always evaluate for tiered delivery (see Step 5.5)\n136\t\n137\t### Epic Generation Rules\n138\t19. Safety-critical strategy (guardrails, sandboxing, RBAC) → generate fail-mode Investigation + security Investigation, both blocking main Implementation\n139\t20. New component not in architecture context → generate onboarding chain: `repo-onboarding` + `license-validation` (parallel start) → `konflux-onboarding` (after repo-onboarding) → general implementation (after license-validation; parallel with konflux-onboarding). For new container image in existing repo: skip repo-onboarding, start with image build Implementation + `konflux-onboarding` (parallel).\n140\t21. External community dependency where team submits PR/RFC and acceptance gates downstream → generate upstream Implementation epic, evaluate tiered delivery. If viable fallback exists (cherry-pick, fork) → note as AC, not separate epic. If third party resolves → model as precondition with tiered delivery, no separate epic.\n141\t22. Infrastructure not in platform inventory → generate validation Investigation (does it exist/work?) + provisioning Implementation\n142\t\n143\t### Acceptance Criteria Rules\n144\t23. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic\n145\t24. `docs-authoring` epic → add \"technically reviewed against implementation\" AC\n146\t25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add \"build pipeline green\" AC\n147\t\n148\t## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery\n149\t\n150\tWhen an external dependency has uncertain timing:\n151\t\n152\t1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?\n153\t2. **YES** → Split into:\n154\t   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)\n155\t   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)\n156\t3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream\n157\t\n158\t## Step 6: Classify Epics\n159\t\n160\tFor each epic, determine:\n161\t\n162\t### Type (mandatory)\n163\t- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)\n164\t- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)\n165\t\n166\t### Implementation Type (optional routing label)\n167\t\n168\t| Label | When to apply |\n169\t|-------|--------------|\n170\t| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |\n171\t| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |\n172\t| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |\n173\t| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |\n174\t| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |\n175\t\n176\t### AI Implementability Signals\n177\t\n178\tScore signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.\n179\t\n180\t#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)\n181\t\n182\tEvaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.\n183\t\n184\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |\n185\t|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|\n186\t| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope (\"improve X\") |\n187\t| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |\n188\t| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |\n189\t| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |\n190\t| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |\n191\t| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |\n192\t| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |\n193\t| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |\n194\t| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Strategy cites specific architecture context files/APIs | Unsubstantiated architecture claims |\n195\t\n196\t#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)\n197\t\n198\t**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.\n199\t\n200\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |\n201\t|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|\n202\t| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |\n203\t| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |\n204\t| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |\n205\t| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |\n206\t| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. \"is this ADR approved?\") |\n207\t\n208\tThe pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.\n209\t\n210\tWrite the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.\n211\t\n212\t## Step 6.5: Health Warnings\n213\t\n214\t### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)\n215\t- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)\n216\t- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent\n217\t\n218\t### Handling unclear strategy passages\n219\t\n220\tWhen the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:\n221\t\n222\t| Situation | Handling |\n223\t|-----------|---------|\n224\t| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |\n225\t| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |\n226\t\n227\tWhen a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, \"if X requires changes to Y\"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.\n228\t\n229\t## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria\n230\t\n231\tEach epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:\n232\t- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope\n233\t- HLRs mapped to this epic\n234\t- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)\n235\t- Rules 23-25 from Step 5\n236\t\n237\tEvery AC must be a testable pass/fail condition on THIS epic's own deliverable. External schedule constraints are not ACs: turnaround you do not control (accredited-lab queues, review-board cadence, upstream vendor timing) belongs in the epic's Risks/Notes or the summary's Health Warnings. Write the AC at the engineering completion point you do control — \"the evidence package is submitted to the certification lab and triaged\" is a valid AC; \"lab scheduling and review-board cadence are externally controlled and cannot be compressed\" is a schedule-risk note misfiled as an AC.\n238\t\n239\t## Step 8: Generate Artifacts\n240\t\n241\t### Step 8a: Write decomposition summary (the plan)\n242\t\n243\tWrite the decomposition summary **first** — this is the blueprint for all epic files.\n244\t\n245\tWrite `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md` in two steps:\n246\t\n247\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections:\n248\t   - **Epic List** (table: ID, title, type, team, priority)\n249\t   - **Dependency DAG** (Mermaid `graph TD` diagram — roots at top, arrows point from dependency to dependent: `E001 --> E003` means \"E001 must complete before E003 can start\")\n250\t   - **DAG Justification** (table: edge, rule, rationale)\n251\t   - **HLR Traceability Matrix** (HLR → epic mapping, confirming full coverage)\n252\t   - **Health Warnings** (priority inversions, scope traps — if any)\n253\t   - **Tiered Delivery** (if applicable — Tier 1 vs Tier 2 split)\n254\t\n255\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n256\t\n257\t```bash\n258\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \\\n259\t    parent_strat=\"{ID}\" epic_count=<N> critical_path_length=<N>\n260\t```\n261\t\n262\tAdd `triage=<value> triage_rationale=\"<reason>\"` for triaged strategies (Step 0).\n263\t\n264\t### Scope constraint: decompose, don't design\n265\t\n266\tYour job is to break strategy scope into units of work, not to make implementation decisions.\n267\tIf the strategy describes a capability at a functional level, the epic scope stays at that level.\n268\tDo not invent API paths, URL schemas, response formats, environment variables, caching policies,\n269\tCRD field names, or other implementation details not stated in the strategy. Those are decisions\n270\tfor the implementing team.\n271\t\n272\t### Step 8b: Write per-epic files\n273\t\n274\tWrite one file per epic to `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN.md` (e.g., `{ID}-E001.md`, `{ID}-E002.md`), following the decomposition summary as the plan. Each epic's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, and HLR mappings must match what the summary specifies.\n275\t\n276\tFor each epic, write in two steps:\n277\t\n278\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections (minimum — add additional sections when the strategy contains relevant content for this epic's scope, e.g., risks, assumptions, open questions, stakeholder commitments):\n279\t   - **Title** (one line)\n280\t   - **Description** (what this epic delivers)\n281\t   - **Scope** (specific changes in this epic)\n282\t   - **Acceptance Criteria** (derived from strategy)\n283\t   - **HLR Traceability** (which strategy HLRs this epic covers)\n284\t   The four section headings are literal and required for EVERY epic, including `docs-authoring` epics — an outline of content topics goes INSIDE the `## Scope` section, never as a renamed `## Content Outline` heading (a renamed heading fails the artifact contract).\n285\t   Signal rationales go in a separate file (see Step 6) — do not include them in the epic body.\n286\t\n287\t   **No cross-references to sibling epics.** Do not reference other epics by draft ID (e.g., \"E001\", \"E003\") anywhere in the body — not in descriptions, scope, acceptance criteria, or HLR traceability. Draft IDs are internal to the decomposition and meaningless once epics are created in Jira. Dependency relationships are captured by frontmatter `dependencies` and Jira Blocks links. Each epic body must be self-contained: describe what it delivers and depends on in plain terms (e.g., \"the OTEL env var injection capability\" not \"E003\") without naming sibling epics.\n288\t\n289\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n290\t\n291\t```bash\n292\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n293\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n294\t    component=\"<canonical name from .context/rhai-components.txt>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n295\t    type=Implementation priority=P0 \\\n296\t    dependencies=\"{ID}-E002,{ID}-E003\" \\\n297\t    ai_signals.change_specificity=1 \\\n298\t    ai_signals.pattern_precedent=1 \\\n299\t    ai_signals.adapter_pattern=0 \\\n300\t    ai_signals.existing_foundation=1 \\\n301\t    ai_signals.open_questions=-1 \\\n302\t    ai_signals.external_dependency=0 \\\n303\t    ai_signals.human_process_gates=-1 \\\n304\t    ai_signals.repo_access=1 \\\n305\t    ai_signals.architecture_claims=1\n306\t```\n307\t\n308\tFor an **Investigation** epic, set `type=Investigation` and write the five\n309\t`investigation_signals` instead of `ai_signals` (do not set both):\n310\t\n311\t```bash\n312\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n313\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n314\t    component=\"<canonical name>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n315\t    type=Investigation priority=P0 \\\n316\t    investigation_signals.question_specificity=1 \\\n317\t    investigation_signals.source_accessibility=1 \\\n318\t    investigation_signals.local_runnability=1 \\\n319\t    investigation_signals.cluster_hardware_dependence=0 \\\n320\t    investigation_signals.human_judgment_required=0\n321\t```\n322\t\n323\tAdd optional fields only when non-null: `implementation_type=<value>`, `branch=<value>`, `gated_by=<epic_id>`, `gate_failure_impact.action=<value> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<text>\"`. Every epic that depends on an Investigation should have `gated_by` pointing to that Investigation (see Rule 3).\n324\t\n325\tDo **not** include `ai_implementability` or `ai_implementability_score` — the pipeline computes those from `ai_signals` (Implementation) or `investigation_signals` (Investigation) automatically.\n326\t\n327\t### Step 8c: Verify consistency\n328\t\n329\tAfter writing all epic files, run:\n330\t```\n331\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py batch-read artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-*E[0-9][0-9][0-9].md\n332\t```\n333\t\n334\tCompare the output against the decomposition summary. If any epic file's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, or HLR mappings diverged from the plan, fix the epic file to match the summary.\n335\t\n336\tThen run the contract validator until it passes:\n337\t\n338\t```bash\n339\tpython3 skills/epic-decompose/scripts/validate_decomposition.py {ID}\n340\t```\n341\t\n342\tIt deterministically checks what downstream consumers enforce and an LLM step can silently get wrong: epic body sections (Description / Scope / Acceptance Criteria / HLR Traceability), `component` values verbatim in `.context/rhai-components.txt`, Rule 11 (docs-authoring blocked by every Implementation epic), and priority inheritance (an epic blocking P0 work is itself P0). It prints one `VIOLATION:` line per problem and exits non-zero. Fix every violation by editing the epic files (never edit the script), re-run, and proceed only once it prints `OK`.\n343\t\n344\tThen, as your **final action** — after every epic file is written, any divergence is fixed, and the validator prints `OK` — mark the decomposition complete:\n345\t\n346\t```\n347\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md decompose_complete=true\n348\t```\n349\t\n350\tThe pipeline uses this field to detect that you have finished. Until it is set, the review agent is not launched. Do not set it earlier: anything you write or edit after setting it may be reviewed in a partially written state.\n351\t\n352\t### Conditional decomposition (when applicable)\n353\t\n354\tIf an Investigation epic has ≤3 bounded outcomes that change downstream structure, write one file per branch epic using the `-BRANCH-<letter>-` filename convention:\n355\t\n356\t```\n357\t{ID}-E001.md                        # Shared epic (the Investigation that selects the branch)\n358\t{ID}-BRANCH-A-E003.md               # If outcome A\n359\t{ID}-BRANCH-B-E003.md               # If outcome B\n360\t{ID}-BRANCH-B-E004.md               # Extra epic in branch B\n361\t```\n362\t\n363\t**Branch epics are not standalone Jira issues.** The pipeline attaches each branch's epics to the gating Investigation epic as a plan document; it does not create them as issues or wire Blocks links from them. Two rules follow, and both are enforced downstream — a branch file that breaks them is silently dropped:\n364\t\n365\t1. **Every branch file MUST set `branch` and `gated_by` in frontmatter** (in addition to the normal epic fields), plus `gate_failure_impact`:\n366\t   - `branch=<letter>` — the outcome label, matching the `-BRANCH-<letter>-` in the filename (`branch=A` for `{ID}-BRANCH-A-E003.md`).\n367\t   - `gated_by={ID}-E001` — the `epic_id` of the **main-plan Investigation** whose outcome selects this branch (must be a real main-plan epic). It **MUST also appear in this branch epic's `dependencies`** — `gated_by` is always a member of `dependencies` (the branch cannot start until the Investigation resolves).\n368\t   - `gate_failure_impact.action=<rewrite|remove|add_remediation> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<text>\"`.\n369\t\n370\t   ```bash\n371\t   python3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-BRANCH-A-E003.md \\\n372\t       epic_id=\"{ID}-BRANCH-A-E003\" title=\"<title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n373\t       component=\"<canonical name>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n374\t       type=Implementation priority=P0 \\\n375\t       branch=A gated_by=\"{ID}-E001\" dependencies=\"{ID}-E001\" \\\n376\t       gate_failure_impact.action=rewrite \\\n377\t       gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<what changes if outcome A does not hold>\" \\\n378\t       ai_signals.change_specificity=1 ...\n379\t   ```\n380\t\n381\t2. **A main-plan epic MUST NOT list a branch epic in its `dependencies`.** Branch epics are not main-plan nodes, so a dependency on one (e.g. main-plan `E004` depending on `BRANCH-A-E003`) resolves to a nonexistent epic. If a downstream unit of work depends on the *outcome* of the Investigation, depend on / `gated_by` the **Investigation epic** ({ID}-E001), not on a branch outcome. If it depends on a *specific* branch's work, it belongs **inside that branch** (as another `-BRANCH-<letter>-` epic), not in the main plan. A branch epic's own `dependencies` MUST include the gating Investigation (its `gated_by`) and may also reference sibling epics within the same branch.\n382\t\n383\tOtherwise, write each branch epic **exactly like a main-plan epic (Step 8b)** — the same body sections (Description / Scope / Acceptance Criteria / HLR Traceability) **and its own separate signal-rationale file** `{ID}-BRANCH-<letter>-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (Step 6, one per branch epic) — in addition to the branch-specific frontmatter above. Today these capabilities depend on an inline vector store provider bundled within the Llama Stack process; removing it (per RHAISTRAT-7474) will break them unless an alternative is available at the platform level.\n19\t\n20\t## Problem Statement\n21\t\n22\tGen AI Studio and Auto Rag currently rely on an inline Milvus provider embedded in the Llama Stack distribution image to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This inline provider runs inside the Llama Stack process itself.\n23\t\n24\tRHAISTRAT-7474 proposes removing inline providers from the Llama Stack distribution to improve GA readiness — shipping only what can be tested and maintained at scale, and aligning with Llama Stack's primary use case as a remote API server. However, no platform-level alternative exists today. If inline providers are removed without a replacement, any RHOAI user relying on Gen AI Studio's RAG capabilities or Auto Rag will lose functionality entirely — there is no workaround short of manually provisioning and configuring an external vector database.\n25\t\n26\tUsers expect vector storage to \"just work\" when they use Gen AI Studio or Auto Rag. The current out-of-the-box experience must be preserved even as the underlying architecture evolves.\n27\t\n28\t## Affected Customers\n29\t\n30\t* All RHOAI customers using Gen AI Studio playground with RAG capabilities\n31\t* All RHOAI customers using Auto Rag\n32\t* This is a platform-level product dependency: these features cannot function without a vector store\n33\t\n34\t## Business Justification\n35\t\n36\t* **Product integrity:** Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag are GA-track capabilities in RHOAI. Removing the inline vector store without a replacement breaks shipped product functionality for every user of these features.\n37\t* **Blocking dependency:** RHAISTRAT-7474 (removing inline providers for GA readiness) cannot proceed until this RFE is resolved. Silas Brenmark (Gen AI Studio lead) has identified this as a blocker.\n38\t* **User experience:** RHOAI differentiates on integrated, opinionated defaults. Requiring users to manually provision and configure a vector database before they can use the playground or Auto Rag degrades the out-of-the-box experience that customers expect from the platform.\n39\t\n40\t## Acceptance Criteria\n41\t\n42\t* \\[ \\] A default vector store is available out-of-the-box on RHOAI without requiring users to manually provision or configure external infrastructure\n43\t* \\[ \\] Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability\n44\t* \\[ \\] Auto Rag functions with the default vector store with no loss of current capability\n45\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the Llama Stack instance (not an inline provider)\n46\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store is scoped appropriately for multi-tenant environments (e.g., per-namespace isolation)\n47\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store is lightweight enough to run in resource-constrained environments without imposing significant overhead\n48\t\n49\t## Success Criteria\n50\t\n51\t* Users of Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag experience no functional regression when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution\n52\t* No additional manual setup steps are required for RAG workflows compared to the current experience\n53\t* RHAISTRAT-7474 is unblocked and can proceed to implementation\n54\t\n55\t## Open Questions\n56\t\n57\t* What is the preferred scoping model — per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both? (Silas noted per-namespace is preferred for isolation, but Auto Rag may need per-instance scoping)\n58\t* Should users have a migration path from the default vector store to a production-grade vector database? (Bram Sundqvist raised the importance of aligning with commonly-used vector DB providers for easier migration)\n59\t\n60\t## Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)\n61\t\n62\t> **Note:** The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: `RHAISTRAT-8004-strategy.md`.\n63\t\n64\t## Staff Engineer Input\n65\t\n66\t**Correction 1 — OGX does not auto-provision PostgreSQL.** OGX defaults to SQLite for storage (`storage.kv.type: sqlite`, `storage.sql.type: sqlite` in the OGXServer CRD). The odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF hardcodes SQLite when creating OGXServer instances for the playground (`kv_sqlite` and `sql_sqlite` in `llamastack_config.go`). PostgreSQL is a supported backend but must be user-configured with an explicit `connectionString` secret. The strategy's claim that \"every LlamaStackDistribution instance requires a PostgreSQL database\" is incorrect — introducing PostgreSQL is new work, not an extension of existing infrastructure.\n67\t\n68\t**Correction 2 — A Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector already exists.** The `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` image includes pgvector out of the box — confirmed in the [sclorg/postgresql-container Dockerfile](https://github.com/sclorg/postgresql-container/blob/master/16/Dockerfile.rhel9) (`INSTALL_PKGS=\"$INSTALL_PKGS pgvector\"`). PostgreSQL 18 (RHEL 9) also includes pgvector. Furthermore, the model-registry-operator already uses `postgresql-16` as its auto-provisioned database image, and `RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected installs. No custom image build is needed. No Konflux onboarding is needed. The 1-2 sprint image onboarding estimate in the strategy can be eliminated.\n69\t\n70\t**Architectural direction — platform-level database vs. self-provisioned.** Multiple RHOAI components now need PostgreSQL (model-registry, MLflow, and now OGX for pgvector). The preferred long-term direction is a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL managed via the DSC, where each component consumes a connection string rather than self-provisioning. A shared platform-provided PostgreSQL via DSC will not be available until RHOAI 3.6. For 3.5, Gen AI Studio must provision its own PostgreSQL instance.\n71\t\n72\t**Operator dependency for self-provisioning (RHAISTRAT-7164).** Self-provisioning PostgreSQL following the model-registry-operator pattern requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio. The ogx-k8s-operator is upstream and cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic. The dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) would provide this operator layer. This is a hard dependency — until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live. It will be challenging to commit this strategy to a specific release until that dependency is delivered.\n73\t\n74\t**Fallback if RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time.** If the dashboard modularization is not ready for 3.5, the fallback is to require customers to bring their own PostgreSQL for RAG capabilities in the Playground. Users would manually configure the OGXServer CR spec with their PostgreSQL connection details. This aligns with the breaking changes introduced in OGX 1.0, even though the Playground largely abstracts OGX from users. The development team should define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning.\n75\t\n76\t**Decouple from Auto Rag.** Auto Rag integration with Gen AI Studio (RHAISTRAT-7824) is targeting RHOAI 3.6. This strategy should validate pgvector only for Gen AI Studio Playground RAG workflows. Auto Rag compatibility with pgvector will be addressed in RHAISTRAT-7824's scope. Remove Auto Rag from affected components, impacted teams, acceptance criteria, and validation requirements.\n77\t\n78\t**Performance and index thresholds — dev experimentation scope.** The default pgvector instance is meant for development experimentation, not production usage. Strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99) are not required. The sprint 1 benchmark should capture the inline Milvus baseline and verify pgvector is in the same order of magnitude, not meet a specific threshold. Typical Playground RAG usage involves small document sets — flat scan (no index) is sufficient for the default. Users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database. Remove open questions about latency thresholds, corpus size ranges, and index type selection.\n79\t\n80\t**PostgreSQL resource sizing.** Reference the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits as the starting point. Adjust based on sprint 1 benchmarking if needed.\n81\t\n82\t**Alternative fallback — BFF-managed PostgreSQL provisioning.** If RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time, an alternative to requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL is to have the gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly, similar to how the BFF currently provisions guardrails infrastructure. The BFF would create the PostgreSQL Deployment, Service, PVC, and Secret when a playground with RAG is configured, if one does not already exist in the namespace. Caveats: (1) the implementation must be designed for portability — when the platform-provided shared database becomes available (3.6), the BFF should consume the shared connection string rather than self-provisioning; (2) lifecycle management of the PostgreSQL instance must be carefully considered — the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation need explicit design attention.\n83\t\n84\t**Existing remote vector store implementation is reusable.** Per the engineering team, the existing remote vector store implementation can be largely reused for pgvector integration. The majority of the work effort is around infrastructure and provisioning of the PostgreSQL/pgvector database, not the vector_io provider integration itself.\n85\t\n86\t**Correction 3 — Vector storage and application storage are independent configurations.** The OGX vector_io provider configuration (`remote::pgvector` via `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`) is completely separate from OGX's application storage backend configuration (`storage.kv.type`, `storage.sql.type`). This strategy only needs to configure the pgvector vector_io provider — it does not change the application storage backend, which remains on its existing default (SQLite). There is no SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration concern because the application storage is not being touched. The root `ogx-k8s-operator` binary runs the OGXServerReconciler, which watches OGXServer CRs (ogx.io/v1beta1) and reconciles each into a Deployment, Service, HPA, PDB, NetworkPolicy, ConfigMap, and optional Ingress and PersistentVolumeClaim. A `configgen` CLI generates runtime configuration from distribution specifications. The root operator (`ogx-k8s-operator`) owns the user-facing OGXServer CR lifecycle, while `ogx-module` manages the platform-level OGX component CRD that the RHOAI operator uses to install and configure OGX itself. This separation keeps the user-facing reconciliation loop independent of the platform bootstrapping logic.\n21\t\n22\tThe OGXServerReconciler owns a broad set of child resources—Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, HPAs, PDBs, NetworkPolicies, Ingresses, PVCs, and Secrets—and uses label-scoped informer caches (`app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: ogx-operator`) to reduce watch pressure on the API server. It also watches Secrets and ConfigMaps with a dedicated label selector rather than listing the entire namespace, which is a meaningful isolation boundary in multi-tenant clusters. A legacy adoption path exists for migrating pre-existing resources under operator management (controllers/legacy_adoption.go).\n23\t\n24\tTLS configuration is delegated to the OpenShift platform: the operator fetches the APIServer TLS profile at startup via `controller-runtime-common/pkg/tls.FetchAPIServerTLSProfile` and applies it to the webhook server, falling back to the Intermediate profile on non-OpenShift clusters or transient API errors. This means cipher suite and minimum TLS version are platform-managed rather than hardcoded.\n25\t\n26\tThe ogx-module controller relies heavily on odh-platform-utilities for kustomize-based manifest rendering, controller condition helpers, garbage collection, and platform detection (ODH vs RHOAI). It manages ValidatingWebhookConfigurations, CRDs, RBAC resources, and Deployments as owned resources, providing full lifecycle management for the root operator's installation. Prometheus monitoring integration is established via RBAC grants on monitoring.coreos.com PrometheusRules and ServiceMonitors.
